title: Jeremiah 50:33–46
context: The LORD of Armies declares that Israel’s Redeemer is strong and will plead their cause (50:33–34), sends a sword on every part of Babylon (50:35–38), and pictures its desolation like Sodom and Gomorrah (50:39–40). Two earlier oracles are reused: 50:41–43 repeats almost word for word the oracle against Zion in 6:22–24, now turned against “daughter of Babylon,” and 50:44–46 closely repeats the oracle against Edom in 49:19–21. Line 50:40 also echoes 49:18. These parallels are named without harmonizing the differences in wording.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says: “The children of Israel and the children of Judah are oppressed together. All who took them captive hold them fast. They refuse to let them go.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD of Armies says, “The children of Israel and the children of Judah are oppressed together.” Arminian readers see God noticing his people’s captivity and their captors’ refusal to release them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the LORD aware of his people’s bondage. The refusal to let them go may recall Pharaoh in Exodus, and readers in this tradition hold that echo as suggestive rather than certain.

verses.text: Their Redeemer is strong. The LORD of Armies is his name. He will thoroughly plead their cause, that he may give rest to the earth, and disquiet the inhabitants of Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes: “Their Redeemer is strong. The LORD of Armies is his name.” Arminian readers see the LORD as kinsman-defender of his people, pleading their cause against their oppressors.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise rejoice in the LORD as Redeemer who will plead his people’s cause. Readers in both traditions commonly see this as shared ground on God’s faithfulness, not as a point of disagreement.

verses.text: “A sword is on the Chaldeans,” says the LORD, “and on the inhabitants of Babylon, on her princes, and on her wise men.
verses.arminianNotes: “A sword is on the Chaldeans,” says the LORD, “and on the inhabitants of Babylon, on her princes, and on her wise men.” Arminian readers see judgment reaching every level of Babylonian society.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the sword falling on rulers and sages. Readers in this tradition note the repeated “A sword is on” as a poetic device stressing the comprehensiveness of judgment.

verses.text: A sword is on the boasters, and they will become fools. A sword is on her mighty men, and they will be dismayed.
verses.arminianNotes: “A sword is on the boasters, and they will become fools.” Arminian readers see Babylon’s boasters, perhaps its diviners, exposed as foolish when judgment comes.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see false wisdom brought to nothing. Who exactly the boasters are is not fully clear, and readers in this tradition hold identifications with diviners or false prophets with caution.

verses.text: A sword is on their horses, on their chariots, and on all the mixed people who are in the middle of her; and they will become as women. A sword is on her treasures, and they will be robbed.
verses.arminianNotes: “A sword is on their horses, on their chariots, and on all the mixed people who are in the middle of her.” Arminian readers see Babylon’s military strength and wealth stripped away.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see every source of Babylon’s security failing. Readers in this tradition see the verse as showing that no human resource can withstand the LORD’s judgment.

verses.text: A drought is on her waters, and they will be dried up; for it is a land of engraved images, and they are mad over idols.
verses.arminianNotes: “A drought is on her waters, and they will be dried up; for it is a land of engraved images.” Arminian readers see idolatry named as a reason for judgment on a land dependent on its waters.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see judgment tied to idolatry. Readers in this tradition note the phrase “they are mad over idols,” which presents idolatry as a kind of folly.

verses.text: Therefore the wild animals of the desert with the wolves will dwell there. The ostriches will dwell therein. It will be inhabited no more forever, neither will it be lived in from generation to generation.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore the wild animals of the desert with the wolves will dwell there.” Arminian readers see the stock imagery of a ruined city returned to wild animals, as in Isaiah 13:21–22.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see desolation pictured with wild creatures. Readers in this tradition read such imagery as prophetic language of judgment, cited alongside Isaiah 13 by reference.

verses.text: As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and its neighbor cities,” says the LORD, “so no man will dwell there, neither will any son of man live therein.
verses.arminianNotes: “As when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah and its neighbor cities,” says the LORD, “so no man will dwell there.” Arminian readers see Babylon compared to the classic example of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the Sodom comparison expressing total judgment. The same line appears against Edom in 49:18, and readers in this tradition note the reuse without harmonizing the two settings.

verses.text: “Behold, a people comes from the north. A great nation and many kings will be stirred up from the uttermost parts of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, a people comes from the north.” Arminian readers note that verses 41–43 reuse, almost word for word, the oracle against Zion in 6:22–24, now turned against Babylon.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see 50:41–43 reusing 6:22–24 nearly word for word, so that the invader later faces the same kind of judgment. Readers in this tradition note the reversal without harmonizing the differences in wording.

verses.text: They take up bow and spear. They are cruel, and have no mercy. Their voice roars like the sea. They ride on horses, everyone set in array, as a man to the battle, against you, daughter of Babylon.
verses.arminianNotes: “They take up bow and spear. They are cruel, and have no mercy.” Arminian readers see the same description once used of Babylon’s army now applied to Babylon’s attackers.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the reversal: in 6:23 the target was “daughter of Zion,” here it is “daughter of Babylon.” Readers in this tradition see measure-for-measure justice in the reused words.

verses.text: The king of Babylon has heard the news of them, and his hands become feeble. Anguish has taken hold of him, pains as of a woman in labor.
verses.arminianNotes: “The king of Babylon has heard the news of them, and his hands become feeble.” Arminian readers see the king experiencing the anguish Judah once felt, as in 6:24.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the labor-pain image reused from 6:24. Readers in this tradition note that what Judah once said of itself is now said of Babylon’s king, without harmonizing the wording.

verses.text: Behold, the enemy will come up like a lion from the thickets of the Jordan against the strong habitation; for I will suddenly make them run away from it. Whoever is chosen, I will appoint him over it, for who is like me? Who will appoint me a time? Who is the shepherd who can stand before me?”
verses.arminianNotes: “Behold, the enemy will come up like a lion from the thickets of the Jordan.” Arminian readers note that 50:44–46 closely reuses 49:19–21 from the oracle against Edom.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise note the reuse of 49:19–21, with Babylon in place of Edom. “… who is like me? … Who is the shepherd who can stand before me?” affirms the LORD’s incomparable rule over all rulers.

verses.text: Therefore hear the counsel of the LORD that he has taken against Babylon; and his purposes that he has purposed against the land of the Chaldeans: Surely they will drag them away, even the little ones of the flock. Surely he will make their habitation desolate over them.
verses.arminianNotes: “Therefore hear the counsel of the LORD that he has taken against Babylon.” Arminian readers see God’s announced purpose against Babylon, echoing words spoken earlier against Edom in 49:20.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise hear the LORD’s counsel and purpose. Readers in this tradition see the reused wording as showing that the same sovereign purpose governs judgment on every proud nation.

verses.text: The earth trembles at the noise of the taking of Babylon. The cry is heard among the nations.
verses.arminianNotes: “The earth trembles at the noise of the taking of Babylon. The cry is heard among the nations.” Arminian readers see Babylon’s fall shaking the world that once trembled before it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the nations hearing of Babylon’s fall. The line closely parallels 49:21 on Edom, and readers in this tradition note the reuse without harmonizing the details.
